Commentary on Sengzhao’s Treatises, Volume One.
Regarding the terms *nirvāṇa* (泥曰) and *nirvṛti* (泥洹): the former refers to taking up that which is without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), while the latter is a transliteration of the path of practice.

*Nirvāṇa* is the unconditioned extinction; *nirvṛti* signifies the completion and exhaustion of cessation. The "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti), in the "Dharma-offering Chapter," speaks of the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa* (般泥洹).

The current scripture speaks of the "extinction of all Buddhas" (*parinirvṛta*). This precisely refers to the state without remainder as *nirvṛti*. As stated in the *Prabhāvatī-sūtra* (放光經): [text follows].
It says: "Nirvāṇa" and "Nirvṛti"—these two names appear interchangeably.
The memorial presented to the Qin King, Lord Yao, refers to Yao, whose clan name was Shun. After composing the treatise, he wrote this preface and presented it to the Qin King, Lord Yao.
"Memorial" (biao) means to present and submit to the King. The preface contains seven points: first, praising the King’s virtue; second, [the meaning of] Nirvāṇa... [and so forth].

1. "The Nirvāṇa described by [Seng]pan" refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. 2. "Sengzhao and those below" are self-deprecating. 3. "And Your Majesty’s praise of the King’s treatise" refers to the Emperor’s commendation of the *Śāstra on the Mahāyāna*.
4. "Able to be a sage and below" indicates relying on the King’s treatise to compose this own treatise. 5. "This treatise has not yet... introduces alternative interpretations. 6. "Now, unfolding...
concludes the composition of the treatise and its presentation to the Sovereign.
Regarding the initial praise of the King’s virtue and the concluding account of Sengzhao’s commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, Master Dao’an’s biography states:
"Since the Wei and Jin dynasties, śramaṇas have taken their teachers’ surnames as their own; thus, their surnames vary.

However, the Dharma Master [Sengzhao] considered that among all masters, none is more venerable than Śākyamuni, and therefore he took 'Śākya' as his clan name. Later, he obtained the *Ekottarika Āgama*, which indeed confirmed this.
It is said that when the four rivers enter the sea, they no longer bear the names of rivers; likewise, those of the four castes who become śramaṇas are all called Śākyas.
This already accords with the sūtras, and thus [the distinction between castes] was forever set at rest.

*Nirvāṇa*, *nièhuán*, and *nírúo*—these are the same as what this treatise calls "Chu" and "Xia" (where the central region is called Xia, and the capital of Nan Yue is called Chu); though the dialects differ, the pronunciation of *nirvāṇa* is correct. (Master Guan and Master Daliang also expounded this meaning. However, one must...

The *Sūtra of the Questions of the True Son of Heaven* states: "One practices within nirvāṇa but does not abide in nirvāṇa; one practices within the realm of death but does not abide in the realm of death.

This is because, O Cāturmahārājika, nirvāṇa is pervasive; whatever is created must have something upon which it relies. Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who compose treatises must first pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Now, Master Zhao has composed this treatise based on the King’s [request] for it to be transmitted throughout the world. For this reason—
First, the virtues of the King are set forth in three sections: first, citing antiquity; second, formal praise; and third, corroborating with the present. Regarding the initial citation of antiquity:
though the words are not employed [here], they are cited because one who praises a Great Man dares not speak arbitrarily;
thus, the established words of the ancients are used to head this chapter. Laozi says: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One..."
"By attaining the One, they find tranquility. The spirit attains the One and becomes numinous. The valley attains the One and becomes full.
The feudal lords and kings attain the One and become stabilizers of the world. Now, it is said that these three [examples] serve as clarifications of the meaning of "the One.

Having cited this ancient saying, he explains this single principle through three different interpretations. Wang Bi states: "The One is the beginning of numbers and the ultimate of things; each is itself a distinct entity."
This is why it is taken as the primary principle. Thus, the "Tian Di" chapter of the *Wai Pian* states: "That from which the One arises is the One itself, yet it has not yet taken form.
Guo Xiang’s commentary explains: "The One is the most subtle state at the very beginning of duality. That from which the One arises arises from the Ultimate One;
it does not arise from nothingness. He Shang Gong says: "The One is non-being (wu); it is the child of the Dao. Indeed, this is concise and fundamental.
The preface to the text states: "First is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Wood has the emptiness of wood, and names have the emptiness of names; thus, the divergence and convergence arise spontaneously.
If we discuss the internal meaning, it is that non-abiding through causes and conditions constitutes 'one'."

The second section, beginning with "I humbly reflect," is a formal eulogy consisting of four pairs of eight-character phrases. The phrase "I humbly reflect upon Your Majesty" (*fówéi biànhà*) is the general heading. Regarding the term "Han":
the *Záshì* (Miscellaneous Matters) states that "Han" is the designation for the realm under heaven; the designation for the realm under heaven is "Emperor" (*huángdì*).

He refers to himself as "Zhèn" (*zhèngzì yuē zhèn*), while subjects address him as "Biànhà. Cāoyōng says: "The Son of Heaven is so honorable and noble that one dares not speak of him directly; therefore..."

Addressing the Emperor as "Your Majesty" is roughly analogous to using "Your Honor. The first two pairs of four-line verses praise the essence (*tǐ*) and its function (*yòng*), as well as the object (*jìng*) and wisdom (*zhì*).
The latter two pairs of four-line verses praise the discernment of the occasion (*zhī jī*) and the composition of the treatise (*zuò lùn*).

The phrases "Profound wisdom and reverent clarity; the Way meets with the spirit" praise the essence and function. "Profound wisdom and reverent clarity" praises the essence (the *Xici* says: "The ancient one who was intelligent, wise, virtuous, and sagely was always profoundly knowing; only the Martial One possessed this").

"Sixth, it is the state of not decaying. "Yì" (睿) means sagely, penetrating, and wise. "Zhé" (叡) is the character for wisdom (pronounced *dīng-liè*). "Qīn" (欽) means reverence, beauty, a grand appearance, and also contemplation.
The phrase "The Way unites with the spirit" (*dào yǔ shén huì*) praises its function. "The Way" refers to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) that are cultivated;

it signifies being in accord with the mental spirit such that there is no duality between them. Regarding "spirit" (*shén*): it is drawn from the sense of "penetrating" (*shèn*). It reaches everywhere and cannot be measured or known by spatial dimensions; therefore, it is called "spirit. Furthermore, that which is unfathomable in both its hidden and manifest aspects is termed "spirit."
"Exquisitely attuned to the center of the ring; there is no principle it does not encompass. These two phrases constitute the second pair.

These two phrases cite the object to praise the wisdom: "the center of the ring" is the object, and "exquisite attunement" is the wisdom. (The *Zhuangzi* says: "Right and wrong revolve and pursue one another without end; therefore it is called the 'center of the ring. The center of the ring is empty.)
Now, taking "is" and "is not" as a ring, that which attains its center is devoid of "is" and "is not. If one discusses internal meaning, the center is not the emptiness within the ring;

if the emptiness within the ring were taken as the center, then emptiness would possess a distinct substance [from the ring]. The first two lines clarify that the factors of the path cultivated in practice are non-dual with the mind and spirit;
these two lines clarify that the path cultivated in practice is non-dual with the objective realm. "Is" and "is not" constitute...

"Circle. There is neither right nor wrong; this is the "Middle. The circle is the conventional (sāṃvṛta), and the Middle is the ultimate (paramārtha). This statement describes the wondrous harmony between the ultimate and the conventional.

Since one has realized the ultimate and the conventional, there is nothing the circle does not encompass; hence it is said that "there is no principle it does not unify. Alternatively, the preceding phrase may be taken as referring to the ultimate.

The second line refers to the mundane world. The two subsequent pairs of four lines—“Wielding the blade amidst the myriad affairs” (*you ren wan ji*) and so forth—praise the one who knows the opportune moment (*ji*) and the composition of the treatise.

This line specifically praises the wisdom that illuminates the opportune moment. Regarding “wielding the blade amidst the myriad affairs,” the *Zhuangzi*, in the chapter on “Nourishing Life” (*Yang Sheng Zhu*), states:
“When Cook Ding was dismembering an ox for Lord Wen Hui, his blade moved as if newly whetted. Thus, of the nineteen uses of his blade, [it remained so].

In a single year, he mastered several thousand characters. Where there is space between the joints, the blade passes through without resistance; where there is space for entry, the extraordinary must necessarily have room to move.
By this metaphor, one who knows the pivot preserves their life-force. To propagate the Way all day long—this phrase clarifies that the Way is not abandoned.
Throughout the entire day, amidst ten thousand involvements, the Way is not forsaken. Relying upon and covering all living beings, he transmitted the texts and composed his works.

"Then" refers to the second pair [of verses], which formally praises the composition of this treatise based on its intended audience. This line clarifies the virtue of the Sage for whom it was written.
"Clothing and covering the myriad things" refers to providing support and shelter. This is why they are so favored. The character for "clothing" (yī) is pronounced *yú*;

the character for "covering" (pèi) is pronounced *fú*. Regarding "providing for the beings in the granary": a military depot is called a *kù* (armory), while a grain depot is called a *cāng* (granary). *Cāng* means to store. As the *Śāstra* says:

The granary is a metaphor for the body. Through the causes and conditions of a practitioner’s bodily karma, seeds are sown and enter the granary; when these causes and conditions ripen, one obtains a human body.
The hemp, wheat, and other grains within the granary are precisely the various kinds of impurities within the body.

Just as a farmer opens the granary and sees the various different seeds, so too does the eye of wisdom open to see the impurities within the granary of the body. To say that the belly stores grain means...

Regarding the birth of this [treatise]: "To transmit texts and establish rules" is the phrase that precisely clarifies the composition of the treatise. Composing the text with one's own hand is the meaning of "transmitting" (chui);
providing a standard for future generations is the meaning of "establishing rules" (zuoze).
Section Three. Now follows the lower-level realization within the realm, which properly concludes by extolling the virtues of the King.
Regarding the "four greats," these four pervade both heaven and earth. As for why they are called "great": although all things are abundant, none are greater than heaven and earth.

Thus, when the fire-kalpa (tejo-bhaya) burns and heaven and earth are first separated, once heaven and earth are divided, there exists the human being therein. Among humans, none are greater than the King; therefore, it is said: [as follows].
These are the three greats. The Dao is that which pervades and gives birth to the myriad things; therefore, it is the greatest. Thus it is said that there are four greats within the realm (*yù*).
Regarding the distinction between the Dao and the realm, Wang Bi states: "Generally, all things have names, and none are not the limit (*jí*) of their own nature.

To speak of the Dao as having 'no' [name] is because there is a source from which it arises. Only after this source exists can it be called the Dao. If this is so, then the Dao is the greatest of all measures. It is not... [the end of the fragment].
If there were nothing greater than the scale, it would have no name and could not be designated. "Domain" (*yu*) means a boundary; it refers to the limits of a territory.
If one discusses the internal meaning, these four are all within ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), where non-abiding is the foundation;
therefore, it is said that "within the domain there are four greatnesses. This "one" refers to the first in the numerical sequence.
The second meaning praises the principle of *nirvāṇa*. It consists of two sections: first, praising its function; second, from "miao mang" (vast and boundless) downward, praising its essence.

Here, "the path of *nirvāṇa*" refers to *nirvāṇa* at the stage of fruition as the path. "The path that accords with the spirit" refers to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) cultivated as the path.
"The path of constant expansion" refers to all causal and resultant states, objects and wisdom, existence and non-existence.
"Taking these as the Way": regarding that which is the ultimate destination of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), there are two possible interpretations for praising the principle through the practice.

First, it means that although the Three Vehicles differ, they all ultimately return to the Way of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Second, it means that all Three Vehicles realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

since the unconditioned is non-dual, it is called their "destination. "The deep reservoir of the Vaipulya [sūtras]": this praises the principle by citing the teaching. "Deep" (*yuan*) refers to water.

"Deep place" (*shenchu*): a location where many fish gather. "Treasury" (*fu*): a storehouse; a place where wealth and goods are concealed. It is also called a "treasury" because it is a place where officials reside together.
This is explained through two meanings: first, it is said that the practice of causes arises from the teaching, and the fruit is established based upon that practice.

Therefore, it is called the "place of assembly. One interpretation states that because the scriptures clarify the myriad virtues of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), it is called the "profound treasury" (*yuanfu*).
Second is the praise of the essence (*tattva*): "Miaomang" (眇莽) means that when one looks into the distance, the vision is hazy; when the eyes lack clarity, it is called "meng" (䁎). Master Yuan said:

To gaze profoundly into ignorance is like the dawn breaking upon a short night; it is like being asleep yet not yet awakened. Zhuangzi said: "To gaze profoundly" refers to the piercing of a rhinoceros horn.

By riding upon the multitude and shattering through the ten thousand things, one is thus able to remain constantly unimpeded whether emerging or dwelling, free from any ground of stagnation or narrowness.
When looked at, its form is invisible, which is called "the Even" (Yi); when listened to, its resonance is unheard, which is called "the Sparse" (Xi). Yet, even so—

"Vastly remote, rarefied, and silent" indicates that the realms and wisdom are transcended. "This is called a domain" means that the domain of conditioned phenomena differs from the aforementioned domain of ultimate emptiness;
this refers to the meaning of two domains: existence and non-existence. "Profound, subtle, and mysterious" describes the cessation of mental activity.
The third meaning concerns self-humility. It consists of two sections: first, the presentation of the precepts received; second, the further clarification of self-humility.

Regarding the section on receiving the precepts, there are three parts: first, expressing self-congratulation; second, presenting the precepts received; and third, clarifying the specific precepts undertaken.
The phrase "humbly receiving the grace of the state" expresses this self-congratulation. This sentence celebrates being granted the royal command. The word "humbly" (猥) means—

"Once more": first, he was commanded to leave the household life; second, he was commanded that Sengzhao, Daorong, Huiri, and others should assist Master Kumārajīva in the definitive establishment of the sūtras and śāstras.

Hence it is said, "once more received. Regarding the phrase "dwelling in leisure at the academy," this sentence celebrates his inclusion among the students. Zheng Xuan said: "To expound the principles of filial piety, one must reside in the lecture hall.
When two attendants serve him, it is called 'dwelling in leisure' (xiánjū); when three attendants serve him, it is called 'residing' (jū)."

"Yin" means a mat. Wang Su says: "Zengzi was attending alone; as he sat in leisure, he expounded upon filial piety, hence it is called 'Leisurely Dwelling' (*xiánjū*). 'Dwelling' (*jū*) means abiding.

'Successively' (*cì*) refers to his time under the gate of Master Shi, where he formally went out to receive instruction for more than ten years. Regarding 'ten or more years,' in the reckoning of summer months, a year is termed a *suì*."

"Year" (*sui*) means "to arise. "To arise" implies a limit. In the Yin dynasty, a year was called *zai* (carrying); "carrying" refers to carrying forth all things. In the Zhou dynasty, a year was called *nian* (year);
"year" means "to advance," for what is new advances. Now, being under the gate of Master Shi, one attains reality through a humble breast; thus it is called *zai*.
Although later various scriptures present different approaches, this clarifies what has been studied. Regarding the phrase "different approaches," this clarifies the scriptures.
The essential meaning is not uniform. As for "the superior destinations are not one": the *Prajñāpāramitā* is signless (*animitta*), while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* leads all to the same end;
each is a superior destination, as it is said to be the "king of all sutras. Although the superior destinations are not one, the ultimate goal (*mūla*) and teaching (*śāsana*) is *nirvāṇa*.
This is the second section. Regarding the first part, which is Hui Zhao’s self-deprecation, there are three segments: first, his self-deprecation; second, clarifying the composition of the treatise.
This is the reason for it. Later, he lamented that his teacher had departed from the world. Regarding the phrase "talent is obscured and insight is meager": "talent" (*cai*) refers to ability;
"insight" (*shi*) refers to the wisdom cultivated through past practice. "Instruction" (*hui*) means teaching or analogy. [The master] still harbored a sense of "vast obscurity. The *Yupian* states:
"Vast obscurity" (*mo-mo*) describes the manner of accomplishment; it also implies stability, tranquility, and detachment—the appearance of peaceful composure. This speaks of how talent is obscured.
My own intelligence is short; I have gained nothing at all. From "Next, [my] ignorance was exhausted without ceasing" onwards, it describes the gradual process of composing this treatise.
Although my ignorance has not yet been fully exhausted in the presence of the Master, the fundamental principles of the doctrine remain intact, and I seem to possess some understanding.

However, because I have not yet shown where the eminent and victorious foundations of the Great Name were first established, I have remained undecided within myself. From "Afterward, unfortunately... onwards, he laments the passing of the Master.
"Worldly Master: If Master Shi were still alive, I would have dared to resolve any points of doubt or contention. Since the Master has passed away, there is no one left to consult.
In the latter part of this passage, I have followed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* and ventured to compose a commentary modeled after the Ten Wings of the *I Ching*."

The fourth section is the Discourse Praising the King. It consists of two parts: first, the discourse praising the king; second, from "I am not... onwards, teaching how to accord with the Great Being.

Within the main praise, there are three sections. The first clarifies that one who possesses the essence and function does not harm speech and sound. The second clarifies the core tenet of the discourse.

The subsequent conclusion clarifies that there is no [intrinsic] mark. Regarding the statement "sagely virtue is not solitary," the *Lunyu* says: "Virtue is never solitary; it will surely have its neighbor.
Furthermore, the *Wenyanyan* (Words on the Text), in its commentary on the first hexagram line of Kun, states: "The noble person resolves with rectitude within and acts with righteousness without.

When reverence and righteousness are established, virtue is not solitary. This means that Your Majesty and Master Shi possess virtues that are neighbors to one another; therefore, it is said that [virtue] is not solitary.
Regarding "the Way exists in what is witnessed with the eyes": Zhuangzi said, "One comes having seen what is to be seen; one departs having heard what is to be heard.
Zhongni (Confucius) said, "In such a person as this, the Way exists in what is witnessed with the eyes; the eyes move slightly, yet the mind attains it.
Zilu said, "Master Kong has long wished to see Zi Xue. Now that he has seen him, why is it that he cannot speak of him? Zhongni—

It is said: "In the case of such a person, the Way exists within the very act of beholding; it cannot be contained by words. This is because the intention of the scholar has already been conveyed through his own composition.
Consequently, he was able to set forth the principles of the luminous doctrine. Tradition states that Emperor Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty possessed a profound and mysterious affinity for the Way;

he directed his mind toward the Buddha-dharma and dedicated his will to the Mahāyāna. He then composed the *Tong sanshi lun* (Treatise on the Three Times), which eternally establishes the principle of cause and effect.

From the princes and dukes down to the commoners, they all followed his influence. Among them, Shan Gongxian and Ancheng Hou Song were prominent; their cultivation of the causes and conditions for faith placed them within the ranks of the assembly.
To rectify principles and propagate the teachings was called "shaking the profound wind" (*zhèn xuánfēng*); it may also be said that Buddhism is the profound wind.
Now, the establishment of both birth-and-death and nirvana is entirely due to craving and desire. Once craving and desire have ceased, birth-and-death [ceases].

To sever [samsara] forever is called *nirvāṇa*. Regarding "the spirit is hidden in the profound Han," the *I Ching* says, "The hidden dragon: do not act. This means that the Sage corresponds to the nameless;
as for the nameless Sage, the Sage has yet to manifest his merit, and his traces are not something that can be known through analogy. He is "hidden."

It is profound. It is vast. It is a treasury. It is supreme. It is contemplation. It is the manifestation of discernment. "Mysterious" (*xuan*) means that within the cavernous silence there is nothing.
Regarding "emptiness and space conjoin with its virtue": the non-existence of birth and death is *nirvāṇa*, just as the non-existence of the myriad things is empty space;
therefore, it is said they "conjoin with its virtue. Following this, the term "*nirvāṇa*" concludes the section on signlessness, as the text explains.

This can be seen. Section Two. From "Were it not for his Way being equal to those below" down to "is the same as a Great Being," there are three parts: first, citing two Great Beings to compare them with the King;
second, manifesting their attainment of liberation and awakening; and third, clarifying the model for future generations. Regarding the phrase "acting as a rampart for the Dharma":

Mañjuśrī is the ancestral teacher of Śākyamuni; now acting as his disciple, they mutually complete the teachings. This is like a city where the flow of water serves as no obstacle, and the surrounding earth forms a moat.
The Great Teaching’s ultimate purpose is further revealed here: it clarifies that when the Dharma of Śākyamuni perishes, Maitreya will appear in the world. Furthermore, this is clearly demonstrated.
Next, by examining and playing with [the text] below, it clarifies that awakening is attained in the present. How much more so does what follows clarify this?
This serves as a guide for future generations.
Regarding the fifth meaning, this treatise is composed based on the *Rājanīti-śāstra* (Treatise on Kingship). It consists of two sections: first, the reasons for composing the treatise;

second, the actual production of the treatise itself, beginning with the phrase "Now, [I] compose... The reasons for composing the treatise are divided into three parts. The first part clarifies these reasons by means of both principle (*tattva*) and scripture (*āgama*).
Next, regarding the two types of persons—the ignorant and the wise—this explains the reason [for the preceding]. Afterwards, analogies are cited to construct the treatise.
"Principle and teaching": the Sage’s intent is profound and mysterious; this phrase clarifies that the principle of the King’s treatise is deep. "The principle is subtle and the words are concise";

this phrase clarifies that the teaching regarding the principle is obscure. The section beginning with "Furthermore, it cannot... explains the reason by means of the two types of persons, the ignorant and the wise. First, the advance...
The "High Gentleman" (gāoshì) refers to the wise person; "Tí" (提) refers to the foolish person. The *Liáo* (Lí sāo) says: "Alas, you little one! You do not yet know what is good or bad.

This means that instructing him face-to-face—speaking directly to his ears and admonishing him—is essential. The subsequent lines are intended to provide examples for the purpose of composing this treatise.
Regarding the "Ten Wings" (Shīyì): one interpretation states that the first is called the *Tuán* (彖). *Tuán* means to break or analyze; it subsequently analyzes the hexagrams.

Regarding the various meanings therein: second is *xiàng* (image). *Xiàng* takes "modeling after the phenomena" (*fǎxiàng*) as its meaning; that which exhaustively represents the phenomena modeled by the hexagrams is called *xiàng*.

Third is *Wényán* (Explanations of Words); fourth is *Xìcí* (Appended Statements); fifth is *Kuàngguǎ* (Hexagram Comparisons); sixth is *Xùguǎ* (Sequence of Hexagrams); and seventh is *Záguǎ* (Miscellaneous Hexagrams). There are only these seven.
To speak of "many" as being "ten": regarding the *Zu* (Wings), Confucius took the seven parts of the former sages and added three of his own.

The "three" refer to Fuxi’s hexagrams, King Wen’s hexagram judgments (*ci*), and "Yuan, Heng, Li, Zhen"; the "ten" refer to King Wen’s line judgments (*ci*), such as "Qian-jiu: Hidden Dragon; do not act.
Thus, the name "Ten" arose from Confucius, which is why they are called the "Ten Wings" (*Shi Yi*). How could he have sought to covet elaborate literary schematics?
"To extensively manifest the profound intent" constitutes the reason for composing this treatise; this is the second section.

Next, I shall formally present the treatise itself, which consists of three parts corresponding to the three preceding sections. From the beginning up to the "reliance on the analogy of proof," this corresponds to the preceding [section on] principle and scripture.
This constitutes the "Exposition on Making [the Treatise]. Next, from "I respectfully recount" down to "may it correspond in the distance," the author addresses his superior, saying:

"It is like a person recounting a treatise. Regarding the phrase "divine mind": this refers to the divine mind of Your Majesty. Now, having thoroughly investigated my thoughts and deliberations, they are not yet sufficient to correspond in the distance;

I shall hereafter briefly employ them as a model to provide a comparison for my superior, thereby concluding the treatise I have composed. As for the "Mysterious Gate" (*xuánmén*): Laozi says, "The Mysterious within the Mysterious."
The Gate of All Subtleties. Zhuangzi says: "Entering and exiting without its form being seen—this is called the Heavenly Gate. This gate has four meanings:
first, the teaching as the gate to principle, for the teaching elucidates principle; second, the object as the gate to wisdom, for wisdom arises by means of the object.
The three powers constitute the gate to the ultimate reality; they open the gate of expedient means to reveal the true aspect.

The four types of liberation constitute the gate to nirvana, just as the ten stages constitute the gate to the fruit of Buddhahood. "Mystery" (xuan) refers to the principle that is profoundly silent and devoid of marks;
"gate" (men) refers to the meaning of universal arising without obstruction.

The sixth meaning critiques divergent schools. It consists of two sections: first, an exposition of the *Wanglun* (Treatise on Kings); second, the actual [critique], as clarified below, concerning the benefits and harms, which is the phrasing of Master Zhao.

The exposition of the *Wanglun* has three parts: first, the presentation of divergent interpretations; second, the critique based on common sense, beginning with "My... and so forth; and third, the refutation according to principle.
Regarding the critique based on common sense, the *Wanglun* states: "This is far too extreme. This refers to the passage beginning with "Xiao... [the *Xiaoyao You*].
Yao said: "Jianwu asked Lianxuan, 'I heard from Jieyu that there are those who are vast yet without practical application, who go forth but do not return.
I am struck with awe and alarm; they seem so remote as to be beyond human feeling. What were their words? [Lianxuan replied:
'On Mount Langgusha there dwells a divine person, whose flesh is white as ice and snow, and whose appearance is as pure and refined as that of a young maiden.'"
They do not eat the five grains; they inhale the wind and drink the dew. They stand upright because they are upright and do not believe in [worldly] things.

It is said that when the Sage seizes the opportunity, he is not yet greedy, just as when the fragrance of burning incense spreads. Yet those who are deluded cannot believe this, claiming it is a matter of transcending the mundane and proceeding directly, unbound by human sentiments.
Later, if there were no Sage, who would know what is non-existent? This is precisely to rely upon principle.

This concludes the second section. Following "In truth, as the clear words [state] below," Master Zao’s response to the preceding explanation of loss and gain consists of three parts, which likewise correspond to the three preceding sections.
First, he explains based on conformity to refute the opposing schools. Second, he clarifies loss by contradicting worldly sentiments to critique them from the perspective of those sentiments.
Third, he clarifies gain by conforming to [the truth] to refute [the views] based on that conformity. Within the vast and profound void...

Regarding "the essence" (*jing*): Laozi says, "Vague and indistinct, yet within it there is essence. The Donggong says, "To manifest form where there is no form is to take the vague and indistinct as the ultimate attainment.
Regarding "the profound and deep" (*yao-ju*): this describes the state of principle being so far-reaching and boundless that it is difficult to perceive.
The commentary states: "That which is profound and obscure may be considered non-existent; yet within it there is essence (*jing*). This 'essence' refers to what is spoken of externally:

when the mind turns back from the extreme of obscurity and exhausts principle to the fullness of its nature, this is called 'essence. Therefore, the Eastern Palace says: 'If it differs from the Great Void, it is so called;

how much more so regarding internal principles and teachings? Following the passage beginning with 'the various scholars,' they act contrary to their feelings to clarify what is detrimental, hesitating as they proceed."

The appearance of not advancing refers to a state of dejection; it is the condition of the mind being dissatisfied. Later, "fortunately meeting those below" means following [the teachings] with clarity and benefit.

Regarding the phrase "those who knock at the gate," Master Rui’s *Preface to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Master Kumārajīva possessed a heart of wisdom that awakened like the wind; his enduring influence resounded far and wide.
The King of Qin knocked at his empty gate, and Master Jiaofu [匠伯] set forth its profound depths. This was during the age of the Final Dharma.

The commencement of this [attainment] begins here. Regarding "entering the profound chamber" (*weideng xuan shi*), Master Yuan said: "In name, one is foremost among those who have entered the chamber;

in practice, one's traces are as severed from the mundane as dust. This refers to the fact that worthy men (*xianren*) are those who have ascended to the hall, while sages (*shengren*) are those who have entered the chamber. *Wei* (蔚) is pronounced *yú guì*.
This describes the flourishing appearance of grasses and trees. Zhi Daolin, in a letter to a Daoist from Gao-li, said:

"The brilliant and luxuriant middle-class [beings] are already established as suns and moons. Xu Guang stated that "shì" means "substance"; things are contained within its substance. As for "the Wheel of Dharma turning twice":

The teaching is likened to the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), which is explained through three meanings: first, the subduing of sentient beings, just as a king’s golden wheel can subdue the four quarters;

second, the destruction of the thieves of afflictions (kleśa), just as a king’s golden wheel [subdues] brave and wicked men; third, the transformation of the lower into the higher, just as the king’s wheel ascends from below to above.
As for the essence of the wheel, both the object (ālambana) and wisdom (jñāna) constitute its essence. Regarding "turning," it is as follows:
To speak and then act is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Because Śākyamuni [is counted] as two, it is said that he did so "twice. Regarding "clouds reflecting," Master Yuan stated:
"The Ultimate Way reflects upon the current year."

The seventh meaning provides a summary of the treatise, consisting of three sections. First, from "Now I expound this treatise" (*jin yan lun*) onwards, it clarifies the core tenet (*lun zong*) of the treatise.

Second, from "Swiftly supporting" (*ji fu*) onwards, it clarifies what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected. Here, we do not adopt the view of "the vast void devoid of sages," but rather adopt only the "Ultimate Person" (*zhiren*), thereby setting aside those who dwell outside the conventional world (*fangwai*).
Third, from "Itemizing" (*tiaodie*) onwards, it concerns serving the Superior (*shangzhe*). As for "as follows" (*ru zuo*), this refers to that which I call "As-It-Is" (*ru*).

As stated below: "Left" means "below. It signifies receiving, serving, following, and transmitting. ○ The first ten chapters of the *Yankai-zong* (Expanding the Opening of the School) consist of nine sections.
This is precisely the exposition of the body of the treatise, which comprises ten explanations and nine refutations. Therefore, Master Huiyuan said: "Nine..."
"Zhe" (折) means "to bend. It also means "to unfold," "to expand," "to propagate," or "to draw near. It is also a term for a water gate. That which does not emerge gradually is not called "yan" (演);
because it now gradually unfolds the school's tenets, it is called "yan. "Zhe" carries the meaning of "bending" or "folding. It is also a word for "discarding wealth," and it implies "curving.
One bends it to attain the center, and bends it further to form the partial. Thus, Dharma Master Rui’s *Preface to the Madhyamaka-śāstra* says: [text follows].
This is to resolve [the matter] by means of the Middle Way. The general purport of the opening section is that the intent of the words is difficult to represent.
Therefore, I shall first describe Master Kumārajīva’s threefold view of the Buddha according to the meaning of the text. Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu asked:

"If the Buddha preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas within the Dharmakāya, and it is only the Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas who are able to see him, then [the Buddha] must possess the four great elements and the five sense organs."
"What is the distinction between the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and [the dharma-body]? Furthermore, a sutra states: 'The dharma-body neither comes nor goes;
it has no arising or ceasing, and its appearance is identical to nirvāṇa. How can it be seen, and yet one preaches the sutras? Master Kumārajīva replied:

"The Buddha’s dharma-body is like a transformation (*nirmāṇa*); it consists of the four great elements and the five sense organs. Nevertheless, the sutra says that there are three kinds of dharma-bodies. The first is..."

The true reality of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) neither comes nor goes; it is identical to nirvāṇa—unconditioned and uncreated. Second is the body of the nature of phenomena (dharmatākāya) through sublime conduct:
this is the true Dharma-body, which, like the sun, pervades the entire Dharma-realm with its radiance, illuminating immeasurable lands.
The sound of its preaching of the Dharma shall encompass the ten directions, and only Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are able to hear this Dharma. Third is...
From this Dharma-body, there is skillful manifestation and transformation, appearing in accordance with the various distinctions among the classes of sentient beings, just like the light of the sun.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the lifespan of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas; he is none other than Śākyamuni.
Now, regarding the intent of opening the school: it is precisely to discern the Nirvāṇa of the Dharma-nature-born body of wondrous practice. This...
The Buddha of the Body Born of Sublime Practice neither comes nor goes; this is precisely the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma-body. There are four meanings for opening the school:
first, explaining the meaning based on the name, which corresponds to the second section, "Distinguishing Names," in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning); second, from "I have once...
onwards, the formal discussion of the meaning of Nirvana being nameless, which corresponds to the third section, "Namelessness," in the *Xuanyi*; third, from "The Sūtra says... onwards, citing...

Regarding the commentary on the meaning of the sūtra and śāstra: "Fourth, 'then' and below" refers to the application of the sūtra. Because the sūtra being expounded is used to name the person who can explain it, it says, "The Nameless One."

The explanation of the meaning based on the name consists of two sections: first, the explanation of the name and meaning of *nirvāṇa*; second, the clarification of the "with remainder" and "without remainder" [nirvāṇas]. Regarding the explanation of the name:

it is translated as "extinction and transcendence" (*mie-du*), and it is also correctly termed "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the explanation of the meaning: "unconditioned" takes the sense of emptiness, quiescence, and stillness.
"Empty" refers to the emptying of the mind; "non-existent" refers to the absence of form. The cessation of wisdom is "quiescence"; being tranquil and still is...
"Vast and desolate" (*mo*) refers to that which is empty-minded and formless, where wisdom is extinguished and there is tranquil stillness; this explains the meaning of "wondrously non-existent.

"Wondrously transcending the conditioned" (*youwei*) explains that it is not existent, nor is it subject to the three marks of existence; therefore, it is said to "wondrously transcend the conditioned."

"Nirvāṇa (nirodha) is also the wondrous non-existence. Great affliction constitutes the fruit; the four flows constitute the cause. When the accumulation of cause and effect is exhausted, [nirvāṇa is attained]. The four flows are:

the flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of views, and the flow of ignorance. Here, 'extinction' (nirodha) is explained through the sense of eternal cessation, while 'crossing over' (pāra-gata) carries the meaning of transcendence.
Guangzhai said: "Extinction refers to the layered state of non-existence, while crossing over refers to being bound within existence. This meaning applies to both persons and phenomena. This...

The phrase "the covering below" provides a dual explanation through analogy for the meaning of unconditioned *nirvāṇa*. "That to which mirror-images return" explains the meaning by way of function (*yòng*).
"The profound abode beyond measure" explains the transcendence of marks (*xiàng*) by way of essence (*tǐ*). These two meanings—essence and function—are used to explain the analogy.
First, as for essence, it is said to be ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), which is like a mirror. Images are, in this context, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); thus the Sūtra says: "It is like..."
It is like an image in a mirror. Why? Because the principle is fundamentally pure, as pure as a clear mirror.

Due to the initial mind of ignorance, one becomes deluded regarding ultimate emptiness, giving rise to karma and nirvana and constructing birth and death. Once the winds of karma have subsided, the mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since the mind is unconditioned, it transcends the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), just as waves naturally subside to become pure water. Question: If that is so, then [the nature of] water...

Qing asked: "When water begins to move, it forms waves; when the wind ceases, it returns to clarity. Yet, while the movement of water results in turbidity, there is no separate 'original clarity' apart from it.

If both turbidity and clarity were to exist simultaneously, one would fall into the tenets of the True School (the Tathāgatagarbha). The Master replied: "Secondly, it is like an image in a mirror: when it comes, it has nowhere from which it emerges;
when it departs, it has nowhere to which it goes. Internally, the case is the same. This triple-world house of fire is ablaze with the eight sufferings; now, as for this fire..."

The dwelling is fundamentally non-burning; now that nirvana is attained, it likewise lacks the characteristic of extinction. It is like a reflection in a mirror, which has no characteristics of coming or going.

Thus, when one speaks of "extinction" (nirvāṇa), one says that it is not extinction; it does not mean that there is an extinction. When one speaks of the "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta), one says that it is not existence;
it does not mean that there is an unconditioned. This is called the absence of any efficacy for grasping objects; objects have nothing to correspond to.
The names correspond to the realities; yet, as for the characteristics of these names and realities, there is nothing to which they correspond.
They ultimately return to the abode of cessation. This is the second section, clarifying the "remainder" and "non-remainder. This is a brief indication of the principle of resonance (ganying).

Truly, these are alternative names for "leaving and dwelling," and provisional designations for responding to things. As the *I Ching* says: "In the way of the noble person, whether leaving or dwelling, speaking or remaining silent, they do not deviate from their [inner] principle."
Although their manifestations differ, their Way is the same and thus they respond accordingly; hence it is said: "The dragon appears in the abyss while dwelling there;

the thunder resounds in the void while remaining silent. (Sang’s commentary states: "When emerging, he is the Son of Heaven; when abiding, he is the common people. Both are attained through spontaneous ease (*anābhoga*), not through deliberate effort. The present meaning is likewise so:
although the fundamental and the manifested differ, both the *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* [nirvāṇas] are provisional.

Regarding the title: although the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku) differ, they are both equally devoid of name and form; they are spoken of through provisional names and forms. Thus, Master Yuan said: "The profound [reality] does not conform to any direction;

the manifested trace transcends both extremes. Now, I shall clarify three meanings: first, both from the perspective of the manifested trace, one clarifies the existence or non-existence of the remainder;

second, from the perspective of the Dharma-body, one distinguishes the existence or non-existence of the remainder as wondrous existence and wondrous non-existence; third, discussing the fundamental and the manifested together. This is what is meant by "emerging."

There is another [interpretation]: "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) is itself "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). The sūtras and śāstras speak of three kinds of conventional designations (*prajñapti*):

first, the conventional designation of causal formation (*hetu-samutthāna-prajñapti*), which involves continuity and mutual dependence; this merely discusses how all phenomena are formed through mutual dependence and does not concern the present context.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of three conventional designations: first, the designation of dharmas (*dharma-prajñapti*); second, the designation of experience (*upabhoga-prajñapti*); and third, the designation of names (*nāma-prajñapti*). The reason these three conventional designations are taught is that the Buddha...

He commanded Subhūti to explain his own intention, saying: "If Prajñā-pāramitā is profoundly penetrating and signless (*animitta*), then there is no Bodhisattva to be taught, nor is there any Prajñā to be expounded. How, then, can one teach a Bodhisattva to practice Prajñā?
The Buddha replied: "Prajñā exists only as a name; the Bodhisattva also exists only as a name. This name does not exist within."
It does not exist externally, nor does it exist in between. What is called "a bodhisattva practicing prajñā" is merely a conventional designation based on the three [falsities].

Previously, it was said that one returns to the profound abode; this was from function returning to essence. Now, regarding both the remainder and the remainderless, it is from essence giving rise to function.

Function does not function by itself; it functions because of its essence. Essence does not constitute essence by itself; it constitutes essence because of its function. Although essence and function are distinct, they ultimately converge in non-duality.
They may also be understood as being mutually relative through their mutual inclusion and exclusion.
The second meaning correctly establishes that *nirvāṇa* is nameless. Above, by relying on names to explain meanings, the "wondrous non-existence" (*miao wu*) was correctly explained;
here, it also concurrently examines "wondrous existence" (*miao you*). This consists of two sections: first, because there are no forms or characteristics, mental activities (*citta-vicāra*) cease;

second, "yet, moreover," citing persons as proof. The first section has three parts: first, clarifying that the characteristics of the mind are largely forgetful; next, using empty space as a metaphor for non-existence; third—[the remainder].
The world [is thus]. The subsequent section distinguishes it from empty space (*ākāśa*). The four characters "silent, desolate, empty, and vast" clarify that there is no form or appearance.

The four characters "subtle, wondrous, and without marks" certify the cessation of mental activity. Following this, with the passage beginning "Transcending all existence," the empty space is used as a metaphor for the Perfected Person (*tathāgata*).
The description "eternally transcending birth and death" is why it is called "transcendence" (*chao*). Because it is neither bright nor dark below, it is called "mysterious ascent" (*you sheng*).
To illustrate its characteristics, it is further said to be like empty space for a long duration. The final three phrases clarify that it does not belong to the three periods of time.

The next phrase clarifies that there are no three marks (*trilakṣaṇa*). Because it cannot be seen by following after it, there is no past; because it cannot be seen by meeting it head-on, there is no future;
and because it is not encompassed within the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*), there is no present. As for "the power of the burden," this refers to the three marks. Zhuangzi said:
"There is no power greater than transformation, yet ordinary people do not know it; they attempt to think about it while deeply concealing it."
The difficulty reaches its ultimate depth. Though things are identical, none dare prohibit their transformative changes; thus, those who conceal and possess them cannot restrain their elusiveness.

Those who do not conceal but allow transformation to proceed naturally cannot be changed by such transformations. Therefore it is said: "Even the strength of one who carries a mountain on his back cannot transform his own body.
Below, in the section on distinguishing differences, it is said: "Vast and boundless emptiness is non-active as if non-existent; it is hazy and indistinct."
The formless is as if present. The "five eyes" (*pañca-cakṣus*) are the five types of vision. The ears are divided into two, namely those of devas and those of humans.
[Xue] [Xue]—profoundly deep. Who sees? Who hears? The *Zhuangzi* says: "One gazes upon the colorless [Xue] [Xue]; one listens to the soundless [Xue] [Xue].
Within [Xue] [Xue], one alone perceives clarity; within the soundless, one alone hears harmony. *Xiao* means "deep."
"Mi-lun" (The Pervasive) refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); it is profound within the profound, exhausting its very source.
"There is nowhere it does not exist" means that its principle pervades all things. Dongkuozi asked Zhuangzi, "Where does the Dao reside? He replied, "It resides nowhere.

Dongkuozi said, "If that is so, then [the Dao] must reside in ants. Zhuangzi said, "Leave them to the ants. Dongkuozi asked, "How lowly! Zhuangzi replied: [The text continues with the dialogue regarding the nature of the Dao.]
"In the tiles and walls. "How much more so? "In excrement and urine. Dongkuozi did not respond. Zhuangzi said:
"Your question, Master, does not reach the substance. You ask for its location where there is no action and no place; therefore, I have not reached the substance with my answer.
This is precisely when form and name are severed, mind and knowledge are extinguished, and seeing and hearing vanish—yet it is not that they do not exist.
The Way may indeed be said to transcend both existence and non-existence.

This is the second section. Now, the following cites persons as testimony; the preceding directly elucidated the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Since both words and characteristics are utterly transcended, we now cite persons and phenomena as proof.
"Phenomena" refers to the four propositions regarding the existence or non-existence of wisdom. Whenever one wishes to establish words and discuss principles, there is no...

Transcending these four, speech is immediately lost and words are cut off; knowing is immediately reversed and the mind is extinguished. This term "this" (ci) signifies the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
To speak of "knowing" refers to its function, while "existence" and "non-existence" pertain to its essence. Next, four individuals are cited as witnesses;
thus, the ultimate is entrusted to the four sages to symbolize that principle transcends all marks. This is because having words about the wordless is not equal to being wordless within the wordless.
It is said that this is why he remained silent while flowers rained down. Regarding Śākyamuni’s “closing his chamber” at Magadha, the seventh fascicle of the *Śāstra* (Treatise) states:
"After the Buddha attained the Way, for fifty-seven days he remained in silence and did not preach the Dharma. He said to himself: 'My Dharma is exceedingly profound and difficult to understand.
All sentient beings are bound and attached to worldly dharmas; none are capable of understanding it. It would be better to remain in silent stillness.'"

This refers to entering *nirvāṇa*. Regarding "stopping the mouth": in the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality" of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, when the various sages and bodhisattvas questioned Vimalakīrti, Vimalakīrti remained silent and did not answer. This was the proclamation of "non-explanation.

When the Buddha commanded Subhūti to transmit the teaching, he expressed his own intention, saying: "The *prajñā* is penetratingly clear and signless; there is no bodhisattva to be taught, nor is there any *prajñā* [to be taught]."
"If it can be described, how can one cause it to function? The Buddha replied: "Prajñā has only a name; the Bodhisattva has only a name.
This name does not exist internally, nor does it exist externally, nor does it exist in between. It is merely a conventional designation based on the three [types of] provisional constructs.

A Bodhisattva abiding in the twentieth stage attains the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and, before becoming a Buddha, is fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha and so forth.
By means of great wisdom-power, they extensively deliver sentient beings without yet becoming a Buddha; like Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and others, they are called "Buddhas" and "Buddhas of Lifespan.

Within this, there are two difficulties: first, regarding the Buddha as one still in training (*śaikṣa*), there is the difficulty of [the state] being incomplete (*sopadhiśeṣa*); second, regarding the Buddha as one whose training has been completed and who has passed away.

This returns to the theme of non-action (*wuwei*) to address the remaining difficulties. The text contains three points: first, defining the reality through its name to extend the intent of the Sūtra;
second, from "I request" (*qing*) downward, each section addresses the remaining and non-remaining [difficulties]; third, from "However, that is" (*ran ji*) downward, it addresses them both together.
Regarding "defining the reality through its name": names reside in phenomena, while designations reside in speech; they do not arise spontaneously but must depend on a reality that can be named.

"Name" refers to Śākyamuni; "title" refers to virtues such as the Ten Powers. "Returning to the source" means that from the perspective of the fundamental essence, it is *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder);
"the divine way" means that based on the traces [of manifestation], it is *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder).
The second section, the "Distinction of Meanings," contains two parts: first, objections with remainder; second, objections without remainder. Regarding the first, the objection with remainder:
when the Tathāgata’s Great Enlightenment and Dharma-body are initially established, the meaning is explained as the severing of delusions, though the three schools differ on this point.

One school asserts that at the moment of the Vajra [samādhi], the severing of delusions is complete and the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not continue to sever anything further; however, because the impermanent reward-body (*vipākakāya*) has not yet perished, it is called "learning from the Buddha."
Master Daliang, Master Ai, and Master Min, along with Wen and others, all employ this explanation. A second view holds that only at the time of Buddhahood are delusions exhausted;
thus it is said that "they are severed by Buddha-wisdom. This is the position employed by Master Ru, Master Zong, Master Zang, and others.

A third view holds that delusions are exhausted at the conclusion of the *vajra* stage, where Buddha-wisdom serves as liberation, and one realizes the eternally abiding [nature]. This is the view of Master Yao and Master Dan.
Master Yun and others all employ this explanation. Regarding the Dilun masters, there are two views.

One says that at the stage of the Diamond-like Mind (vajropama-citta), the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa) and the obstacles to nirvāṇa are entirely exhausted, while the Buddha’s wisdom exhausts the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa).

Another says that at the time of the Diamond-like Mind, both the cognitive obscurations and the obstacles to nirvāṇa are entirely exhausted. Among these three interpretations, it is not known which meaning Master Sengzhao has adopted.
Master Kumārajīva’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, in the section concerning the Bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-duality, states:
"The wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) must exhaust the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) before it finally comes to rest. Regarding this single passage, two schools dispute its meaning.

One school adheres to this text, asserting: "It does not say that the Buddha exhausts the dharma-nature; therefore, we know that the *vajra* [samādhi] is what exhausts it. The other school asserts: "Only the Buddha exhausts the dharma-nature."

This is so. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* cites the explanation of those who advocate sudden enlightenment (*tunwu*), stating that at the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), one suddenly severs all delusions.
Yet, Master Shi Dao’an’s *Youyi lue* (Brief Discussion on Doubts) states: "Sarvajña refers to attaining the One;
through diamond-like wisdom, one simultaneously achieves all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). There is nothing known and nothing unknown. Now, this treatise says: "Shining upon Sarvajña..."

The "darkness-illuminating candle" (youzhu): this refers to the wisdom of the *vajra*, which illuminates that which is most obscure. This is the fulfillment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Once the knowledge of all modes is fulfilled, there are no delusions that are not exhausted; this is the meaning of the exhaustion of delusions. Yet, because retribution has not yet been exhausted, it is therefore impermanent. Master Sheng also said:

second, the provisional trace (*upāya-vṛtti*). Regarding the actual practice: when a Bodhisattva sits beneath the tree and enters the tenth stage, known as the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*), it is like a great cloud pouring down rain continuously;
from the uninterrupted mind, immeasurable and boundless pure Buddha-dharmas naturally arise. Thus one reflects.
Contemplating the immeasurable, he emits light from between his eyebrows to subdue the demonic adversaries. The Buddhas of the ten directions celebrate his meritorious achievements.
When the Sage emits light from between his eyebrows, it enters the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head. The merits of the ten stages are transformed into the Buddha’s wisdom;
all [obstacles to] nirvana are severed, and he attains unimpeded liberation. This is the great wisdom of the ten powers and all Buddha-dharmas. As for the provisional traces:

That is to say, because the Bodhisattva practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) through the power of skillful means, they transcend the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) up to the Bodhisattva stage and abide in the Buddha stage.

To return to emptiness means to return to the true, signless (*animitta*) nirvāṇa; it does not mean that returning to emptiness consists in the annihilation of the body and the extinction of wisdom.
Why? Because the text says: "Transcendently, one is forever separated from the multitude of existents; in its totality, one is merged with..."

It shares the same essence as the great void. Furthermore, it departs together with the void, forever vanishing so that its destination is unknown. Therefore, wisdom does not mean that what was formerly existent has been extinguished;
rather, it is the adamantine retribution coming to an end and returning to the ultimate true *nirvāṇa*.

When form and wisdom both vanish, there is no resting along the long journey. That which is on the feet is called a shackle (*zhì*); that which is on the hands is called a manacle (*gù*). A man without feet said to Lǎo Ān: "Kǒng..."
As for me, I have not yet surpassed the Perfected Man (zhiren). Why do you so earnestly insist on the long duration of my studies? Do you not realize that these [studies] are but shackles?
The scripture says "below," which serves as proof that there is no further difficulty; this may also be taken as evidence from the traces [of the teaching].
The third meaning consists of a double conclusion to the two difficulties, which comprises three sections. First, regarding the "track" (*guǐchè*):

this establishes the thesis and concludes the difficulty, setting forth the great intent of the teaching and clarifying its vast utility. "Dian" (典) means a classic; "jing" (經) means a scripture; "gao" (誥) means an announcement of the Dharma. "Guǐchè" (軌轍) refers to a track or path. [Note:

The counter-criticism is useless. [The character for] "shēng" (聲) is pronounced as "shījiǎo" (尸角反). [The character for] "dài" (歹) is pronounced as "wàijiānzhīyǎnfù" (外堅之掩覆). The *Yì* says: "Among those suspended in the sky and manifesting brilliance, none are greater than the sun and moon.
